classification.difficultyReason: Devise a natural-number encoding for arbitrary finite subsets and prove it distinguishes every subset, including the empty set.

content.prompt: Previously it was established that the set of all subsets of $\mathbb N$ is uncountable. Prove that the set of all finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ is countable.

answer.short:
The set is countable.

Encode each finite subset by a product of prime powers; unique prime factorisation makes this an injection into $\mathbb N$.
answer.worked:
Let $X$ be the set of all finite subsets of $\mathbb N$, and let $p_1,p_2,\ldots$ be the primes in increasing order. Write each nonempty subset uniquely as $S=\{n_1,\ldots,n_k\}$ with $n_1<\cdots<n_k$. Define $f:X\to\mathbb N$ by
$$f(S)=p_1^{n_1}p_2^{n_2}\cdots p_k^{n_k},\qquad f(\varnothing)=1.$$
If $f(S)=f(T)$, unique prime factorisation gives the same number of prime factors and the same corresponding exponents. Thus the ordered elements of $S$ and $T$ coincide, so $S=T$. Also, every nonempty subset maps to an integer greater than $1$, so it cannot have the same image as $\varnothing$.

Therefore $f$ is injective. Since there is an injection from $X$ into $\mathbb N$, $X$ is countable.
